name: Tetlow zinc oxide face powder

lead: Zinc oxide powders were used to keep the skin pale and matte. They became a safer alternative to lead-based whiteners, which had been used since antiquity despite being known to be poisonous.
The entry refers to a zinc oxide face powder from the Tetlow name, introduced as a non-toxic replacement in the mid-1800s.

paras: Face powder is dusted over the skin to even tone and reduce shine. Zinc oxide remains an ingredient of mineral makeup and sunscreen.
The lead whiteners it replaced were associated with poisoning. Zinc oxide is described as non-toxic and does not darken in sulfur-containing air.

chain: Zinc oxide powder applied to the face
angle.text: Dusted on the skin, the powder gives a pale, matte finish. It offered the whitening effect without lead.

lead: The Tetlow zinc oxide face powder is described as a non-toxic powder that replaced lead whiteners in 1866. People used it to give the face a pale, even, matte finish, the look favoured in the Victorian period.[1]

Zinc oxide as a replacement for white lead had been proposed around 1782 by Guyton de Morveau, because it stays bright in sunlight, is not darkened by sulfur in the air and is non-toxic.[2] Today zinc oxide is a main ingredient of mineral makeup.[2]

paras: Face powders in antiquity contained lead: Egyptian remains from about 2000-1200 BC contain lead fibres, and Greeks and Romans used lead whiteners such as cerussa. Lead was known to be poisonous but stayed popular.[1] In the Victorian era, women preferred a natural look and zinc oxide powders were used to keep skin ivory-coloured.[1]

Zinc white was accepted in oil painting by 1834 and manufactured in Europe by 1850, partly replacing poisonous lead white.[2] Health concerns over lead powders grew in the 1930s, and the US Food, Drugs and Cosmetics Act of 1938 regulated cosmetic ingredients.[1]

timeline.event: Guyton de Morveau proposes zinc oxide in place of white lead.[2]
Tetlow zinc oxide powder introduced as a non-toxic alternative.
US Food, Drugs and Cosmetics Act passed.[1]
